paper_title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them. Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. llama.cpp restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4. On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this. Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration. 1. Introduction Decision models answer fixed question with one option from fixed set: which of 77 intents, whether premise entails hypothesis, whether an agent should call tool. Their output is probability distribution over those options, and the deployed behavior is the top option. change in the top option is changed business decision. The quantity that matters to an operator is therefore how many decisions build changes, not only how many it gets right. Dutta et al. (2024) make the same argument for language models in general and use flips as the metric. Accuracy hides most of this. Over 31,275 public questions, net change of six questions hid 436 that got worse: that is the 4-bit GGUF build of the 27B model we study, against its BF16 original. 1 On the 9B model, the same build's net change of 114 questions hid 527 that got worse. This split is exploratory, and the full-set results give it for every build. Quantization evaluations rarely isolate the weights. typical comparison runs the quantized build once on serving engine (vLLM for FP8 and NVFP4, llama.cpp for GGUF) and the reference once on another, and attributes any difference to quantization. At least four other things changed: 1. The engine. transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp implement the same architecture with different kernels and accumulation orders. 2. The server instance. We measured on 2026-10-16 that one vLLM FP8 instance reproduces itself bit for bit, while fresh instance with identical flags differs by up to 0.94 in logit. 3. The batch. vLLM is not batch-invariant: the logits of one request depend on what it was batched with. 4. The kernel. transformers 5.x routes the models' Gated DeltaNet layers through decorator that tries three implementations in order: hub kernel, the flash-linear-attention (fla) package and pure-PyTorch fallback. Which one runs depends only on whether package imports, and in the version we used nothing reports which ran. We keep two claims apart throughout. quantized build that answers differently from its BF16 original was changed on purpose: its flips are the price of the memory it saves, and the question is how large that price is. server instance that answers differently from an identically configured instance of the same build was not changed at all. That is nondeterminism, defect to fix rather than price to pay. We report both and never pool them. We measure each source on the same records and report each quantization effect as the paired difference against them. Our contributions: decomposition protocol for quantization comparisons, built on paired flip-rate differences with bootstrap intervals on fixed record set. Measurements of three engines and five weight formats for 9B and 27B decision model on one Blackwell-class device, with every record's output released. Five pre-registered predictions with their outcomes, including the two that failed, and an exploratory rerun of all five on the second model. An exploratory split of every full-set flip into decisions that got worse, got better, or changed from one wrong answer to another, and each quantization effect stated as multiple of the largest non-quantization source. An observation we did not anticipate: the vLLM restart floor depends on the format, but not in fixed order. Clef-flash's floor rises from BF16 to FP8 to NVFP4. Clef's FP8 restart is the quietest of its three, and its NVFP4 restart is the noisiest non-quantization source we measured on either model. llama.cpp's single-sequence decision server has restart floor of exactly zero on both. third instance shows that the vLLM floor also depends on which two instances are compared, while the quantization effect measured against the reference stays within two flips across all three. 2. Related work Flips as the metric. Dutta et al. (2024, "Accuracy is Not All You Need", arXiv:2407.09141) show that compressed models can match the baseline's accuracy while changing many individual answers, 2 and argue for reporting flips. We adopt flips as the primary metric and add the question of how many flips comparison would show with no quantization at all. Wu, Dhiman and Koshiyama (2026, arXiv:2608.06564) explain why the flips happen: quantization shrinks decision margins roughly linearly, and the fitted shrinkage predicts flip rates across 16 models to median of 1.0 point. Our finding that flips concentrate where the reference is unsure is what their account predicts for decision head. Backend variability. Masoudian et al. (2026, arXiv:2608.04714) attribute roughly 39% of the benchmark variability practitioner sees out of the box to the inference backend. Pape, Evertz and Schönherr (2026, arXiv:2605.19537) find that the backend alone moves benchmark scores by up to 16.6 points across five engines, vLLM and llama.cpp among them. Both study generation, and neither studies quantization or server restarts. We measure the backend effect at BF16 as one source among four and set it directly against quantization on the same records. Nondeterminism within server. Thinking Machines Lab (He, 2025, "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference") trace run-to-run differences inside one server mainly to batch variance and release batch-invariant kernels. Yuan et al. (2025, arXiv:2506.09501) report accuracy swings of up to 9% from GPU count, GPU type and batch size. Li et al. (2026, arXiv:2610.42148) find that concurrency alone changes some answers of Qwen3.5 decision workloads in every engine they test, up to 3.2% in vLLM between one and 64 clients. Our restart measurement is different quantity: two instances started with identical flags. Serving context in classifiers. Kasa, Kasa and Negi (2026, arXiv:2610.09111) is the closest work that counts changed decisions. They train 180 text classifiers and measure label changes under changes of batch shape, precision, device and 8-bit quantization against repeatability floor, and they find the changes concentrated at small margins. They leave production engines out of scope, noting that vLLM and SGLang "require their own measurement", and they do not study restarts. That is the case we measure, on two released decision models. Restarts, kernel swaps and quantization. Chen (2026, arXiv:2608.13756) swaps only the INT8 matrix-multiply kernel inside vLLM: each kernel reproduced itself bit for bit across cold restarts at 1.7B, and the two agreed on no generated sequence. Patodiya (2026, arXiv:2609.04748) shows that prefix-cache reuse makes repeated llama.cpp and vLLM runs diverge, and that the divergence grows with quantization, from 37.4% of agentic episodes at F16 to 82.5% at Q4_K_M. Without prefix reuse every run repeated exactly. Our vLLM servers run with prefix caching off, so that mechanism is not behind our floor. vLLM bug report (vllm-project/vllm#58899, 2026-09-27) shows greedy output changing between fresh processes because torch.compile picks fused kernel's reduction configuration by timing it at first launch, and processes that picked the same configuration were bit-identical. second report (vllm-project/vllm#62820, 2026-10-21) shows FlashInfer's FP4 GEMM autotuning changing temperature-0 tokens of 27B NVFP4 model. We test below whether start-up selection of this kind explains our restart floor. Kozyrev and Maiboroda (2026, arXiv:2609.04098) quantize all of Qwen3.8-27B to NVFP4, Gated DeltaNet gate projections included, and find the gates the least sensitive layers. Our builds keep those projections in BF16, which by their account is conservative. Community measurements of these models. Hugging Face model cards already report agreement between quantized Clef builds and BF16. TurinTech (2026) measures ggml-org's 27B Q8_0 and Q4_K_M on 2,000 typed decisions on three GPUs, GB10 among them, at 98.8 to 99.0% and 96.9% same answer. kurcontko (2026) measures the 9B at FP8 and NVFP4 in vLLM on 1,400 records (98.8% and 94.3% agreement) and vLLM BF16 against transformers (99.8%). Our 3 full-set rates agree with theirs: the 27B Q4_K_M flips 3.20% of 31,275 public questions, which is 96.8% agreement. None of these cards sets quantization effect against restart or kernel floor. quantization effect against an engine floor. Lu and Ni (2026, arXiv:2611.12634) make the comparison closest to ours. They predict the KL divergence that int8, fp8 and int4 quantization cause in five generative language models, and they set it against vLLM noise floor of 0.17 to 0.22 nats per sequence, measured by changing the reduction order: other kernel selections, tensor parallelism, batch-invariant kernels. Mismatch, they write, "is only meaningful above the run-to-run noise floor of the serving engine." That is the comparison we make, in different currency and from different floor. Their reruns that reused the kernel selection were bitwise identical, so their floor comes from deliberate changes. Ours comes from restarting servers with identical flags, in two engines, measured in decision flips on decision models, with kernel switch and batch change beside it. We searched on 2026-11-03 (arXiv, 20 keyword queries; the web; the model cards of all 191 Clef derivatives on Hugging Face, with silent kernel selection searched specifically) and searched again on 2026-11-10 (about 470 arXiv abstracts submitted or updated since 2026-10-25; vLLM, transformers and flash-linear-attention issues; the 60 most recently modified Clef models). We found no paper that measures the restart-to-restart decision flips of production serving engine and sets quantization effect against them on the same records. Kernel choice as source of numerical difference is well established (Chen; Kasa et al.; Lu and Ni; vllm#58899). We did not find our kernel-selection case measured anywhere: library that picks an implementation according to which packages import. Since version 5.17.0, transformers warns once when the PyTorch fallback runs (pull request #48185). Version 5.16.1, which we used, reports nothing, and the warning does not cover the choice between the hub kernel and fla. 3. Setup

sections.title: 3.1 Models, hardware and software
sections.content: Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B) are Cloudflare's released decision models (Cloudflare, 2026). Each adds joint schema head that scores question's options. Both are built on the Qwen3.5 hybrid architecture, with full-attention layer every fourth layer and Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2024) in between: Clef-flash has 24 Gated DeltaNet layers of 32, and Clef 48 of 64 (from the models' configuration files). All runs used one NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory) inside NVIDIA's NGC vLLM 26.09 container (CUDA 13.4 forward-compatibility mode). sections.title: 3.3 Tasks
sections.content: Twelve public tasks with fixed, seeded held-out splits, 31,275 questions in total: intent: BANKING77 (3,080; Casanueva et al., 2020) and CLINC150 with its out-of-scope class (5,000; Larson et al., 2019) inference: ANLI R1 (1,000), R2 (1,000) and R3 (1,200) (Nie et al., 2019), and ContractNLI (1,991; Koreeda and Manning, 2021) knowledge: MMLU (5,000; Hendrycks et al., 2020), ARC-Challenge (1,172; P. Clark et al., 2018) and BoolQ (3,270; C. Clark et al., 2019) 5 grounding: RAGTruth (2,700; Niu et al., 2024) agent: When2Call (3,652; Ross et al., 2025) ordinal: SST-5 (2,210; Socher et al., 2013) Each record is posed in Clef's own question schema (choice, yes/no, or ordinal score) with one fixed prompt format, released with the results. We also scored the authors' private operational data: four sets, 13,415 records, 27,738 questions. It plays no part in this report's argument, because nobody else can reproduce it. We report it only as aggregate numbers.

sections.title: 3.4 Comparison unit and statistics
sections.content: The restart repeats and ref-fla ran on the first 200 records of each public task. Every decomposition comparison therefore uses exactly those 2,400 records for every configuration of model. Full-set numbers appear in the full-set section and the appendix. The two units are not interchangeable, so every rate below names its unit. The 2,400 records are the first 200 of each task, not random sample, and they weight every task equally, where the full set weights tasks by size. Weighting tasks equally alone raises each quantized build's full-set flip rate against ref by 1.26 to 1.36 times. On Clef-flash the 2,400-record rates against ref run 1.3 to 1.6 times the full-set rates. On Clef they run 0.8 to 1.2 times, because which records come first moves the rate in both directions (exploratory; analysis/exploratory_checks.md). For each pair of configurations we report: the top-1 flip rate mean total-variation distance (TVD) between the option distributions maximum absolute probability difference the share of records that are bit-identical. That means all logits are equal or, for llama.cpp, all probabilities are equal, because llama.cpp returns full-precision probabilities and no logits. Intervals are percentile 95% intervals from 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples over records with fixed seed (20261015). One resample matrix is shared across all pairs of model, so differences between pairs are themselves paired. Where pair has zero flips the bootstrap interval collapses, and we give the exact Clopper-Pearson interval (Clopper and Pearson, 1934) instead: 0 of 2,400 bounds the rate above at 0.15%.

sections.title: 3.5 Making the kernel observable
sections.content: Because transformers chooses the Gated DeltaNet kernel silently, we made the choice explicit. In torch mode the worker blocks the fla import for its own process, which forces the fallback even if the package is installed. In fla mode it wraps fla's entry points with counters and asserts after warm-up that they actually ran. Every result line records the kernel used. Every 27B result line carries this tag. Six early Clef-flash ref sets predate the tag. Three independent pieces of evidence show they ran the fallback: 6 later torch-mode run reproduced the sweep's stored ref output for ANLI R1 exactly (maximum logit difference 0.0 on 200 questions) fla was never present on the sweep container's library path the first ref-fla run failed precisely because fla could not be imported in that container 4. sections.title: 4.3 What the floor changes
sections.content: The floor is small next to every quantization effect we measured, and at 4-bit it is far from negligible. single-run NVFP4 comparison carries restart noise of up to 20 flips (Clef-flash) or 22 (Clef), against effects of 139 and 136, roughly seventh. On both models the NVFP4 restart is the noisiest non-quantization source we found. The vLLM restart floor depends on the format, but the two models disagree on how. Clef-flash's floor rises with quantization: 0 flips at BF16, 5 at FP8 and 20 at NVFP4. Clef's runs 4, 0 and 22. Its FP8 restart reproduced 95.3% of records bit for bit, where Clef-flash's FP8 restart reproduced 15.0%. The share of bit-identical records does not track the flip count on either model. Clef-flash's BF16 restart is 93.7% bit-identical with 0 flips, while Clef's is 6.7% bit-identical with 4. The pattern we expected after the 9B, floor that rises with fewer bits, does not survive the second model. What does survive is weaker and more useful. The floor is specific to the build and the model, so one noise number per engine is not enough, and each quantized build needs its own repeat. Our working hypothesis after the sweep was that kernel selection or autotuning at server start differs between instances. An engine change and quantization step can cancel on some records and compound on others. comparison that changes both at once reports neither effect correctly. 9 third server instance (exploratory, 2026-11-03). After the sweep we started Clef's FP8 and NVFP4 builds third time (fp8-r3, nvfp4-r3), with the same flags, the same 2,400 records and the same 16 requests in flight. If the restart floor came from two discrete start-up states, such as kernel configuration picked by timing at first launch (vllm#58899), the third instance would match one of the first two record for record. The two-state prediction fails: the third instance differs from both earlier instances on 12.0% of NVFP4 records (289 of 2,400) and 2.1% of FP8 records (50 of 2,400). That rules out the two-state version of the kernel-selection story. larger fixed set, or state that varies with timing, is not excluded by three runs. The NVFP4 floor depends on run conditions, by more than five times: 4 flips between the second and third instances, 22 between either of them and the first. The first instance differs from the later two in two ways we cannot separate here: it compiled its graph from scratch where the later two loaded it from cache, and it scored the full task files rather than the subsets. The 4-flip pair shares the later runs' conditions (warm cache, subset streams) and the 22s compare across changed conditions, so 22 is the conservative bound for the effect-against-floor comparisons, and 4 to 22 is the range replay can move depending on conditions. The first instance's extra differences are spread across every position in each task: of the 224 NVFP4 records where the third instance equals the second but not the first, 120 fall in the first 100 records of their task, so they do not come from where the 200-record subsets end. FlashInfer's FP4 kernel selection is probably not the cause, because the first instance tuned 110 kernel configurations and saved them, and the later two loaded those same 110. sections.content: Flips concentrate where the reference is unsure. On Clef-flash, questions where the reference's top probability is below 0.7 make up 16.3% of the set. They hold 86% of NVFP4's flips, 90% of Q4_K_M's, 98% of FP8's and 100% of Q8_0's. This is the pre-registered H3 result. The highest reference confidence at which any Clef-flash build flipped decision was: Build Highest ref confidence among its flips Q8_0 0.663 0.867 FP8 Q4_K_M 0.941 0.969 NVFP4 At 4-bit there is no clean "never above X" rule: Clef-flash's NVFP4 flips 11 of the 18,125 questions where its reference is at least 90% confident. On the 27B (exploratory), 17.7% of questions sit below 0.7. They hold 99% of Q8_0's flips, 97% of FP8's, 89% of Q4_K_M's and 79% of NVFP4's. Neither 8-bit build flips any question where the 27B reference is at least 90% confident. Q4_K_M flips 4 and NVFP4 28 of those 19,233 questions. sections.title: 4.7 Two models in the same memory (exploratory)
sections.content: At 16.6 to 20.0 GB, the 27B's two 4-bit builds sit within 15% of Clef-flash's BF16 builds (18.2 to 19.1 GB), the analyzer's equal-memory window. On the same 31,275 questions, the 27B at Q4_K_M is 1.45 to 1.46 points more accurate than Clef-flash at BF16 on any of its three engines (for example +1.45 [+1.08, +1.86] against ref). At NVFP4 the lead is 0.82 to 0.84 points. Pre-registered H8 asked different question: 4-bit Clef against 8-bit Clef-flash at equal memory. No such pair exists in this sweep, which the hypotheses section covers. 12 5. Discussion The protocol we would ask of any quantization comparison follows directly from the measurements: 1. Compare inside one engine. Serve BF16 on the same engine as the quantized build. On both models the engine change is smaller than the quantization effect, but it does not add to it in simple way. 2. Repeat the quantized build across restart. The floor is specific to the build and the model. It is zero for llama.cpp on both models, and 0 to 22 flips for vLLM, in an order that differs between the two models. Repeat it more than once and report the largest pair: on Clef's NVFP4 build, three instances gave pairs of 4, 22 and 22 flips, so single repeat can understate the floor by more than five times. 3. Record the kernel that actually ran. Pin or block optional kernel packages. Otherwise an unrelated environment change shifts results by about as much as vLLM restart does. 4. Report flips on paired records next to accuracy, and split them. An accuracy change of -0.20 points was hiding 1.2% of decisions changing on Clef-flash. On the 27B, an accuracy change indistinguishable from zero was hiding 3.2%, and 436 of those decisions got worse. Accuracy is the decisions that got better minus the ones that got worse. Flips are both, plus wrong answers that changed to other wrong answers. Neither number is enough alone. 5. Report the distance from the floor as ratio, and name the denominator. "Exceeds the floor" is threshold, and an operator needs to know by how much. 6. Keep nondeterminism and quantization apart. server that disagrees with itself has defect to fix. quantized build that disagrees with its BF16 original has price to weigh. Calling both "changed decisions" merges the two. Most of this costs few thousand extra inferences per configuration. Our repeats used 200 records per task, 2,400 in all, small fraction of full evaluation. Why llama.cpp is exactly reproducible here. Its decision server processes one sequence at time, so batch composition never varies. That is consistent with the zero floor on both models, but we have not verified the kernel-level reason and do not claim one. 6. Limitations Two models, one family. Both models use the same architecture (Qwen3_5ForConditiona lGeneration) and come from one release. The ordering of sources held on both. The vLLM restart pattern did not, and third model could move it again. One device. Every floor in this report was measured on one GB10, whose FP8 and NVFP4 kernels are young. Other hardware may show different restart behavior. Backend effects elsewhere can be much larger: Pape et al. (2026) report up to 16.6 points across five engines. We read our floor as property of this device and these engines, not as constant. Few restart replicates. Each vLLM floor rests on one restart pair per build, with third instance only for Clef's FP8 and NVFP4 builds. That makes the floor the least certain term in every comparison against it. Replicates at five or more instances per build are the next measurement. 13 Interval width. 2,400 records give exact upper bounds of 0.15% for zero-flip pairs. That is enough to separate every 4-bit effect from the floor, but not to rank the smaller nonquantization sources against each other, and on the 27B it cannot separate the llama.cpp engine change from Q8_0. Batching inside vLLM runs. Quality runs used 16 requests in flight, so each vLLM restart comparison includes differences in batch composition as well as instance differences. We report it as the restart drift real deployment would see, not as instance drift in isolation. Restart mechanism open. The third-instance probe rules out two-state start-up explanation and makes FlashInfer's FP4 kernel tuning an unlikely cause. It cannot separate cold graph compile from the full-file versus subset request stream. Doing so takes cold-cache instance on the subsets and warm-cache instance on the full files. Confounded rerun. ref-r2 combines rerun with batch-size change. The attribution to batch size rests on the bit-for-bit reproduction at batch 1 on Clef-flash, and was not checked on the 27B. Pre-registered thresholds. The decision rules for each hypothesis are given with its outcome in analysis/findings.md. Some carry judgment, such as what counts as "within the range" for N4, and we say where an outcome depends on it. For H2, the rule as written on 2026-10-15 did not say how to combine two 4-bit builds and two models. We added reading on 2026-10-23, after the 27B results were seen, and it is dated as such. 7. Pre-registered hypotheses Hypotheses H1 to H11 were registered on 2026-10-15 for the benchmark as whole, before any result existed. Outcomes are as findings.md scores them. H2 and H8 involve both models; the rest are scored on Clef-flash. H1 to H11 and the five tests N1 to N5 are separate registrations, two days apart. Two of them overlap. H1 asks N1's question of both 8-bit builds, and H7 is N3. N2, N4 and N5 have no counterpart. Where the two overlap, the pre-registered tests section gives the test as registered and this section scores the hypothesis as findings.md defines it. Hypothesis Outcome H1 H2 H3 H5 H6 8-bit is indistinguishable from BF16 within the noise floor 4-bit loses accuracy, more on Clef-flash than Clef in absolute flips Flips concentrate where ref confidence is low Calibration (ECE/Brier) degrades before accuracy does Out-of-scope detection degrades more than in-scope classification Drift grows with input length, so real-world data drifts more than benchmarks Not supported: FP8 and Q8_0 both exceed their restart floor Mixed (see below) Supported Not supported Mixed: FP8 only. On CLINC150 its out-of-scope recall falls 0.66 points [-1.33, -0.11] while in-scope accuracy holds. The 4-bit builds flip 2.0 to 2.6% of out-of-scope items against 0.2% of in-scope items, but in both directions, so recall does not fall measurably Mixed: grows with length for FP8 and both 4-bit builds (longest input quartile minus shortest: +0.35 points [+0.02, +0.69] for FP8, +1.15 and +1.20 for Q4_K_M and NVFP4); real-world data drifts more for all four builds, but low confidence explains that better than length does 14 Hypothesis Outcome H7 H9 H10 H11 Engine change moves decisions as much as 8-bit quantization At equal memory, 4-bit Clef beats 8-bit Clef-flash on hard tasks but not easy ones Ordinal score questions shift toward the middle under 4-bit confidence-threshold cascade recovers near-BF16 agreement while escalating small fraction GGUF Q4_K_M and NVFP4 differ at the same nominal bit width Not supported (same test as N3) Not evaluable (see below) Supported, and the shift is small: 0.013 to 0.129 of scale point Mixed: 17 to 18% escalation gives 99.5 to 99.7% agreement on public tasks; the authors' private data needs 26 to 30% Supported: Q4_K_M is 0.59 points more accurate [0.37, 0.81] H2, mixed. The rule is checked for each 4-bit build on the full public set, each model against its own BF16 reference. Three of the four builds lose accuracy (Clef-flash NVFP4 and Q4_K_M, Clef NVFP4). Clef's Q4_K_M does not: -0.02 [-0.20, +0.16]. The second clause holds for Q4_K_M, where the 27B flips 1,000 decisions against Clef-flash's 1,108. It fails for NVFP4, where the 27B flips 1,502 against 1,426. On the authors' private data the 27B flips fewer decisions for both 4-bit builds (917 against 2,425 for Q4_K_M, 1,195 against 2,168 for NVFP4). That comparison is reported beside the rule and is not part of it. H8, not evaluable. H8 needs 4-bit Clef build and an 8-bit Clef-flash build within the analyzer's 15% size window. The closest pair is Clef Q4_K_M (16.59 GB) against Clef-flash FP8 (12.15 GB), ratio of 1.36. The comparison cannot be formed from the builds this sweep made, and no further run of this sweep changes that. Outside the window, and exploratory, the 27B's 4-bit builds lead Clef-flash's 8-bit builds by 5.0 to 6.4 points on the harder half of the tasks and trail by 0.6 to 1.2 points on the easier half. The split is median split on Clef-flash's reference accuracy, chosen after the 27B results were seen. We tested three alternative splits as robustness check: threshold at 80% reference accuracy median split on the mean of both references the median split with its two boundary tasks swapped Under them the hard-task lead is 3.8 to 5.1 points and the easy-task deficit 0.4 to 1.5. The pattern holds in all twelve pair and split combinations. Much of the hard-task lead comes from one task: on RAGTruth alone the 27B Q4_K_M is 14.3 points ahead of Clef-flash FP8, while on SST-5 it is 0.5. 8. Conclusion quantization comparison on production serving stack measures more than quantization. On two decision models and one GB10, sources that are not quantization moved up to 0.92% of decisions: vLLM restart up to 22 of 2,400, and kernel chosen by which packages import 10 to 14. Every 4-bit effect cleared all of them, and 8-bit effects cleared them in 29 of 32 comparisons. Accuracy hid most of what quantization did, because the decisions it made worse and better largely cancelled. The checks that separate these effects cost few thousand extra inferences per configuration: compare inside one engine, repeat each quantized build across restart, record the kernel that ran, and report flips, split by direction, next to accuracy.

sections.title: Code and data availability
sections.content: Code, quantization recipes, build scripts, results and per-record outputs are at https://github.c om/Level5Tech/clef-quant-bench. Quantized weights are at https://huggingface.co/Level 5Tech. Six tasks are released as records: BANKING77, CLINC150, MMLU, ARC-Challenge, BoolQ and When2Call. The other six (ANLI R1 to R3, ContractNLI, RAGTruth and SST-5) are released as record IDs, because their licenses restrict redistribution or do not clearly permit it. datasets/build.py rebuilds every record from pinned upstream revisions. We do not release the authors' private operational data or the project's plan file, so the --private analysis, bench.private_agg and bench.findings below cannot be rerun, and bench.speed omits the private sets when rerun. Their aggregate outputs are in the repository, and the pre-registered text is in PREREGISTRATION.md. Run from the repository root. The first command rebuilds the six tasks released as IDs and needs network access. --models clef-flash python datasets/build.py python -m bench.analyze --records data/records --results results --out analysis/flash_public , python -m bench.analyze --records data/records --results results --out analysis/all_public python -m bench.analyze --private private --out analysis/flash_private --models clef-flash python -m bench.decompose --out analysis python -m bench.decompose --model clef --out analysis/clef_decomp python -m bench.speed python -m bench.hypotheses python -m bench.private_agg python -m bench.findings --root . --out analysis/findings.md python -m bench.restart_probes --records-dir data/records --results-dir results --model clef --out , python -m bench.exploratory_checks --records-dir data/records --results-dir results --out analysis , # exploratory analysis_r3 # exploratory
